userStories.title: Actually delete uploaded objects from storage when a file is deleted
userStories.description: As a customer, when I delete a file I need the bytes gone, because the file-storage edge function deletes the database row and leaves the storage object orphaned forever: the removal call at supabase/functions/file-storage/index.ts:288 is commented out with a note saying 'In production, also delete from Supabase Storage'.
acceptanceCriteria: supabase/functions/file-storage/index.ts DELETE handler removes the storage object before (or transactionally with) the row delete, matching the correct implementation already present at supabase/functions/files/index.ts:220.

Storage removal failure does not silently succeed: the endpoint returns an error, or records a durable retry/tombstone that a sweeper drains. A dangling object must never be reported to the caller as a completed deletion.

Both file endpoints are audited for parity of delete semantics, and the divergence is resolved (one shared helper, or one endpoint deprecated) so behavior does not depend on which URL the client happens to call.

Every other edge function that uploads to storage (branding-profiles, blog-assets, qbr, meeting-transcription recordings) is audited for a matching delete path; each one either removes its objects on delete or is listed in the story notes as a follow-up with a reason.
A backfill script identifies storage objects with no owning row and reports counts per bucket. It reports by default and only purges behind an explicit flag.
An integration or edge test asserts that after DELETE, a subsequent fetch of the storage path 404s.
npm run check && npm run lint pass; deno check passes on every edge function touched.
userStories.notes: [LEGAL / P0] Directly contradicts the deletion right stated in Privacy Policy section 6.1 ('Delete or deactivate your account', 'Signed-in users can export their data and delete...'). Promising deletion and retaining the data is a straightforward FTC Section 5 deceptive-practice theory and a GDPR Art. 17 failure. Evidence: supabase/functions/file-storage/index.ts:277-301, storage removal commented out at line 288; correct sibling at supabase/functions/files/index.ts:207-225. Both write to the 'files' bucket. Note the edge path normalization rule in CLAUDE.md when touching either function. POLICY-COPY RULE (all LEGAL stories, decided 2026-08-17): drafting legal/policy text alongside the code IS in scope, but every changed user-facing legal string must be called out in the commit body under a FOR COUNSEL REVIEW heading so it is reviewed before deploy. IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-18. New shared helper supabase/functions/_shared/storage-delete.ts (removeStorageObjects + removeStoragePrefix) is the single seam; three functions were wrong in three different ways. (1) file-storage: removal was commented out. (2) files: called remove() but DISCARDED the result - supabase-js returns errors in {data,error} rather than throwing, so every storage failure returned "File deleted" with the object still there, which is worse than not calling it. (3) branding-profiles: hard-deleted the profile row and never touched the logos, AND every logo re-upload abandoned its predecessor because keys are minted with a fresh uuid and only the public URL is stored - fixed by listing the prefix, which is the only way to find keys nobody wrote down. Ordering rule applied everywhere: remove bytes FIRST, and refuse to drop the row if that fails, because while the row exists the object still has a reference and the delete is retryable; dropping the row first and then failing loses the only pointer to it. AUDIT of the remaining buckets, per the AC: blog-assets soft-deletes by design and deliberately keeps its object (documented in its own header) - LEFT AS IS because removing bytes would break the restore the soft delete exists for, and the content is marketing images, but note a soft-deleted asset stays publicly fetchable since that bucket is public; qbr and meeting-recordings have NO delete path at all - nothing to fix, listed here as follow-ups. Orphan reporter scripts/report-orphaned-storage-objects.ts (npm run storage:orphans) reports by default, needs --bucket AND --purge to remove anything, and REFUSES to purge when a reference table is missing (files and file_uploads are drift tables in no schema/migration, so their absence would make every object look orphaned). VERIFIED: 14 unit tests on the helper + 4 integration tests that drive the REAL handlers against a stateful fake bucket and assert the object is absent afterwards; proven to catch the original bug by reverting file-storage to the commented-out version (2 of 4 fail, then pass again on restore). tsc holds at 1058, lint 11654 (-262 vs baseline, +15 no-console warnings in the CLI reporter, matching the existing scripts/*.ts convention), build passes, check:edge-paths green. GAP TO KNOW: deno check did NOT run - deno is not installed here and the install is blocked by the agent proxy (403) - and tsconfig.json includes only client/shared/server, so supabase/functions is NOT covered by npm run check either. The edge changes are evidenced by the integration test actually importing and executing both handlers, not by a type check. Run deno check in CI. UNRELATED PRE-EXISTING FAILURE seen while running the suite: server/tests/unit/universal-search.test.ts has 2 failures (expects 6 queries, gets 7); confirmed present with this story stashed, so not caused here and not fixed here.

userStories.title: Extend GDPR erasure to storage objects, not just database rows
userStories.description: As a data subject exercising the right to erasure, I need my uploaded content deleted too, because server/services/gdpr-erasure-service.ts anonymizes database columns and never touches Supabase Storage, so documents, logos, attachments, meeting recordings, and QBR artifacts survive a completed erasure request intact.
acceptanceCriteria: The erasure service enumerates and deletes (or irreversibly anonymizes) storage objects belonging to the subject across every bucket in use: files, branding-assets, meeting-recordings, qbr artifacts, blog-assets.

Objects that must be retained under an Art. 17(3) exemption are retained deliberately, with the exemption named in the erasure report notes, in the same style as the existing backup and audit-log notes at lines ~280-283.
The erasure result payload reports storage objects deleted per bucket alongside the existing per-table row counts, so the completion record is honest about scope.
Erasure is idempotent: a second run over the same subject succeeds and reports zero remaining objects.
A test covers a subject with at least one object in at least two buckets and asserts the objects are unreachable afterward.
The 'Backups excluded from surgical erasure' note is reviewed and kept accurate for storage objects as well as rows.
npm run check && npm run test pass.
userStories.notes: [LEGAL / P1] Evidence: server/services/gdpr-erasure-service.ts has no storage/bucket references at all (grep for storage|bucket|attachment|upload returns only profileImageUrl:null at line 147). It anonymizes users and businessRecords and documents its exemptions well, so the structure to extend is already there. Depends on LEGAL-003 landing a reliable object-delete helper; sequence 003 first. Bucket inventory from the audit: 'files' (files + file-storage fns), 'branding-assets' (branding-profiles/index.ts), 'meeting-recordings' (meeting-transcription/handlers/recordings.ts:15), qbr artifacts (QBR_STORAGE_BUCKET, default 'qbr-artifacts' in the edge fn and 'qbr' in server/routes-qbr.ts:373 -- note the two defaults disagree, which is its own bug), 'blog-assets'. POLICY-COPY RULE (all LEGAL stories, decided 2026-08-17): drafting legal/policy text alongside the code IS in scope, but every changed user-facing legal string must be called out in the commit body under a FOR COUNSEL REVIEW heading so it is reviewed before deploy. IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-18. New server/services/gdpr-storage-erasure.ts, called from executeErasure; ErasureResult gains a storage field with per-bucket outcomes reported alongside the row counts. Separate module because the objects are reached through the Supabase service client, not Drizzle: files, file_uploads, meeting_recordings and the QBR artifact table are DRIFT tables in no schema and no migration, so the code cannot be written against typed models. It probes candidate subject-link columns per table, tolerates a missing table or column, and reports what it could not reach instead of counting it as zero. Bucket scope: files (via files + file_uploads), meeting-recordings (user subjects) and the QBR bucket (customer/lead subjects) are erased; branding-assets and blog-assets are EXCLUDED with stated reasons - they are tenant assets, not personal data, and erasing one subject must not delete the company logo. TWO THINGS FOUND WHILE DOING IT: (1) a test caught a real bug in my own helper - isMissingTableError, mirrored from the edge-function version, falls back to a bare "does not exist" substring which ALSO matches "column x does not exist", so a missing column was misdiagnosed as a missing table and aborted the whole bucket instead of trying the next candidate column. Tightened here. THE SAME LATENT BUG IS STILL PRESENT in supabase/functions/customer-portal/handlers/_context.ts and the billing handlers, where it would make a genuine column error silently return [] instead of surfacing; flagged, NOT fixed here, because changing it touches billing behavior outside this story. (2) AC6 was not a formality: the "backups excluded" note was carried over unchanged and is FALSE for storage - pg_dump does not contain bucket contents, so there is no backup copy ageing out behind a failed object removal. Split into two accurate notes. Also hardened the caller: server/routes-gdpr.ts now leaves the request in_progress and returns 500 when any identified object failed to delete, matching that route existing principle that a failure must not falsely report completion, and the audit event records storageObjectsRemoved + per-bucket detail. VERIFIED: 11 unit tests (multi-bucket deletion asserted against stateful fake buckets, idempotency, failed-removal, missing table, unresolvable link column, tenant-bucket exclusion, subject-type scoping); tsc holds at 1058; lint 11656 (-260 vs baseline); build passes; full server suite 1951 passed with only the 2 pre-existing universal-search failures already confirmed unrelated. HONEST LIMIT: because the referencing tables are drift tables, the candidate link columns (uploaded_by, user_id, customer_id, business_record_id, contact_id) are informed guesses. If none matches the live schema the bucket is reported as unlinked and NOT silently skipped, but someone with live-DB access should confirm the real column names and tighten the specs.

userStories.title: Implement the 30-day post-termination data deletion the Privacy Policy promises
userStories.description: As the company, we need to do what the Privacy Policy says, because section 5.2 commits to deleting or anonymizing account and business data within 30 days of subscription termination and no job in the codebase implements that: the retention engine only covers eleven named tables, none of which are tenant account data or storage.
acceptanceCriteria: A scheduled job identifies tenants whose subscription terminated more than 30 days ago and deletes or anonymizes their account and business data, including storage objects.

Records subject to a longer statutory hold keep their stated retention and are excluded by rule, not by omission: invoices and financial records 7 years, security and audit logs 7 years, support communications 3 years, exactly as Privacy Policy section 5.2 states.
The 30-day window is an export grace period as promised: the tenant can still export during it, and export access is what ends at day 30 alongside the deletion.
The job is registered with the existing cron surface (server/services/cron-service.ts, alongside runScheduledRetention) rather than a new scheduler.
The job is dry-run by default with an explicit flag to execute, logs what it would delete, and writes an audit record per tenant processed.
A test with a fixture tenant terminated 31 days ago asserts the correct tables and buckets are cleared and the exempt categories are untouched.
Privacy Policy section 5.2 is reviewed against what the job actually does, and either the code or the wording is corrected so they match exactly.
npm run check && npm run test pass.
userStories.notes: [LEGAL / P1] Evidence: Privacy Policy section 5.2 at client/src/pages/legal/PrivacyPolicy.tsx:262-272 promises 'for the life of your subscription and up to 30 days after termination, during which you may export your data, after which it is deleted or anonymized'. server/services/data-retention-service.ts IS wired to cron (server/services/cron-service.ts:81 imports runScheduledRetention) and works, but DEFAULT_RETENTION_PERIODS covers only audit_logs, data_access_logs, payment_audit_trail, security_sessions, gdpr_requests, incidents, change_requests, service_tickets, emails, notifications, temp_files. No tenant-termination trigger exists (grep for '30 days' in server/ returns only unrelated billing and briefing windows). Extend the existing service rather than building a parallel one. POLICY-COPY RULE (all LEGAL stories, decided 2026-08-17): drafting legal/policy text alongside the code IS in scope, but every changed user-facing legal string must be called out in the commit body under a FOR COUNSEL REVIEW heading so it is reviewed before deploy. IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-18. New server/services/tenant-purge-service.ts, wired into cron-service.ts beside the existing retention job and following its convention exactly: REPORT-ONLY unless TENANT_PURGE_ENABLED=true. KEY DESIGN CHOICE: the table list is DERIVED from the Drizzle schema at runtime (getTableConfig over every PgTable export, filtered to those with a tenant_id column) rather than written down. There are 501 tenant-scoped tables; a hand-maintained list would be stale within a release, and being stale here means either keeping data we promised to delete or deleting records we are required to keep. Retention is an ALLOWLIST mirroring the Privacy Policy exemptions - financial/tax 7y, security+audit 7y, support 3y, privacy-compliance evidence - so everything else is purged, which is what the promise actually says. FK ordering is solved by retrying failed tables until a pass makes no progress, rather than by a hand-maintained topological sort that would itself go stale. REVIEWING THE DERIVED OUTPUT WAS NOT OPTIONAL AND CAUGHT FOUR REAL ERRORS: (1) five financial tables were scheduled for deletion because the patterns missed them - customer_payments, lease_payments, vendor_bills, auto_invoice_generation and irs_mileage_logs, the last being a TAX record; (2) the security_.* pattern was open-ended and swept in seo_security_analysis, which is SEO tooling, so we would have retained data we promised to delete; (3) the tenant-parent rule read ^(tenants|companies)$ and companies is DEPRECATED CRM DATA (docs/crm-canonical-model.md), so retaining it would have preserved exactly the customer records the 30-day promise covers; (4) after fixing, only seo_audit_history remains in the financial-sounding purge list and it is correctly purged. Final split: 471 purged, 30 held. Lesson: patterns are a safety net for tables added later, never a substitute for reading the generated list - hence scripts/report-tenant-purge-plan.ts (npm run purge:plan), which prints the plan with reasons and highlights anything purge-bound whose NAME suggests a record worth keeping. It needs no DB credentials because classification is pure schema. ALSO: an audit record is written per tenant per run into audit_logs, which is itself a RETAINED table - the evidence that data was deleted has to outlive the data - and a failed audit write is surfaced as an error rather than swallowed, because an unrecorded purge is a deletion nobody can evidence. isWithinExportGracePeriod() derives export cutoff from the same PURGE_GRACE_DAYS constant so the two halves of the promise cannot drift apart. Privacy Policy 5.2 reworded to match what the job actually does (the window is the export opportunity; access ends when it closes). VERIFIED: 13 unit tests concentrated on classification, since that is where both failure directions originate; tsc holds at 1058; lint 11683; build passes; all five guards green; full server suite 1986 passed with only the 2 known pre-existing universal-search failures. NOT EXERCISED AGAINST A REAL DATABASE: no credentials here, so findTenantsDueForPurge and the delete passes are unrun. Review npm run purge:plan output and do a dry-run cycle in staging before setting TENANT_PURGE_ENABLED=true.

userStories.title: Audit storage bucket visibility and move QBR artifacts off public URLs
userStories.description: As a customer, my quarterly business review documents must not be readable by anyone holding the URL, because both QBR code paths call getPublicUrl() on artifacts that contain customer usage and spend data, and no migration in the repo establishes what the QBR bucket's visibility actually is.
acceptanceCriteria: The live visibility of every bucket is captured and recorded in docs/: files, branding-assets, meeting-recordings, blog-assets, and the QBR bucket. This is the first task in the story because the rest depends on it.
QBR artifacts are served via createSignedUrl with a short expiry instead of getPublicUrl, at both supabase/functions/qbr/index.ts:455 and server/routes-qbr.ts:384.
The QBR bucket is private. If it is currently public, existing artifact paths are treated as potentially disclosed and that is stated plainly in the story notes for a breach-assessment decision.
The QBR bucket name disagreement is fixed: the edge function defaults to 'qbr-artifacts' and the Express route defaults to 'qbr'. One canonical name, set in both.
The 'files' bucket is confirmed private, since it holds arbitrary customer uploads; if any code path returns a public URL for it, that path is converted to signed URLs.

blog-assets staying public is confirmed as deliberate (marketing images) and branding-assets staying public is confirmed as deliberate (tenant logos), each with a one-line rationale in the docs note. Neither should hold anything else.

A migration or documented setup step pins each bucket's public flag so the state is reproducible rather than whatever was clicked in a dashboard, following the pattern of drizzle/migrations/_backfill_blog_assets_bucket.sql.
npm run check passes; deno check passes on every edge function touched.
userStories.notes: [LEGAL / P1] UNVERIFIED AT AUDIT TIME: getPublicUrl() returns a URL string regardless of bucket visibility, so the repo alone cannot prove the QBR bucket is public. Confirm against the live project before treating this as an incident. Evidence: supabase/functions/qbr/index.ts:450-456 and server/routes-qbr.ts:373-384 both getPublicUrl. Known public: blog-assets (drizzle/migrations/_backfill_blog_assets_bucket.sql:19 sets public=true, deliberate), branding-assets (supabase/functions/branding-profiles/index.ts:151 createBucket public:true, tenant logos). Handled correctly already: meeting recordings use server-side download() at supabase/functions/meeting-transcription/handlers/recordings.ts:217, not public URLs. POLICY-COPY RULE (all LEGAL stories, decided 2026-08-17): drafting legal/policy text alongside the code IS in scope, but every changed user-facing legal string must be called out in the commit body under a FOR COUNSEL REVIEW heading so it is reviewed before deploy. PARTIALLY IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-18 - LEFT passes:false ON PURPOSE. Three ACs need live Supabase credentials this environment does not have (SUPABASE_URL/SERVICE_ROLE_KEY unset, no .env): AC1 capture live bucket visibility, AC3 confirm the QBR bucket is private and assess disclosure if it is not, AC5 confirm the files bucket is private. Those are the human-gated parts and they are the FIRST task in the story by its own wording, so the story is not done. DONE IN CODE: (AC2) both QBR paths moved off getPublicUrl. The fix is NOT a swap to createSignedUrl at the upload site - a signed URL expires, so persisting one just means a dead link later. Uploads now store the storage KEY and every read mints a 15-minute signed URL; new server/services/qbr-artifact-storage.ts for Express, and the edge fn signs inside toReport, which is the single mapper every read path already goes through. toArtifactKey accepts a bare key OR a legacy public URL so decks written before this keep working. (AC4) bucket-name disagreement resolved: Express defaulted to qbr, the edge fn to qbr-artifacts; both now use one setting defaulting to qbr-artifacts because the edge fn serves production. (AC6) branding-assets and blog-assets confirmed deliberately public with rationale in docs/storage-bucket-inventory.md. (AC7) drizzle/migrations/_pin_storage_bucket_visibility.sql pins all six buckets, following the _backfill_blog_assets_bucket.sql pattern, with a header telling the operator to run the audit FIRST because flipping a public bucket private is a disclosure event, not a migration side effect. NEW TOOL so the blocked ACs are one command: npm run storage:audit lists every bucket, diffs against intended state, and for each public bucket does an UNAUTHENTICATED GET on a real object - because getPublicUrl returns a URL either way, the only honest test is what an outsider actually receives. docs/storage-bucket-inventory.md has a marked placeholder for pasting its output. ALSO FIXED HERE: the LEGAL-004 erasure spec guessed a qbr artifact_url column that does not exist; the real columns are pdf_url and html_url (shared/qbr-schema.ts), now two specs. TWO PROCESS NOTES WORTH KEEPING: (1) esbuild caught a syntax error that a brace-balance check missed - a .replace() with a non-unique needle had wrapped the WRONG call site (qbr suppressions instead of qbr reports). Since supabase/functions is outside tsconfig include and deno is not installed, npx esbuild <file> --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null is the cheapest real syntax gate for edge functions. (2) check-types.mjs reported "errors DECREASED to 5 (-1053)" which was tsc ABORTING on a syntax error in routes-qbr.ts, not an improvement - my import block had been inserted into the middle of a multi-line import. Exactly the false-positive CLAUDE.md warns about; always eyeball an implausible ratchet win. After the repair the count holds at 1058. VERIFIED: 37 tests across the four storage/qbr suites; lint 11664 (-252); build passes; edge-path and migration-journal guards green; qbr edge fn syntax-clean under esbuild. REMAINING FOR A HUMAN: run npm run storage:audit with credentials, paste the table into docs/storage-bucket-inventory.md, apply _pin_storage_bucket_visibility.sql, and if the QBR bucket comes back public treat its objects as disclosed and escalate rather than just flipping the flag.

userStories.title: Complete the subprocessor list and disclose AI processors in the Privacy Policy
userStories.description: As a customer bound by our DPA, I need an accurate list of who processes our data, because Subprocessors.tsx names four vendors while the platform actually sends customer content to roughly a dozen, including OpenAI and Anthropic for document OCR, CSV refinement, meeting transcription, and proposal generation, neither of which is disclosed anywhere.
acceptanceCriteria: client/src/pages/legal/Subprocessors.tsx lists every third party that receives customer or personal data, each with purpose, data categories, and processing location. Verified against the codebase, not from memory.

At minimum the list adds: OpenAI, Anthropic, Sentry, Twilio, ZoomInfo, Apollo.io, DataForSEO, Microsoft (Graph), Intuit (QuickBooks), Google (Places, OAuth), Mailchimp. Each entry is confirmed against a real call site before it is listed.

The Privacy Policy states plainly which product features send customer content to AI processors, what content goes, and that it is not used to train third-party models (verified against the actual vendor terms in force, or the claim is not made).

Privacy Policy section 3.5 (Automated Decision-Making) is kept and extended rather than replaced; it is already accurate about lead scoring and predictive service being decision-support under Art. 22.
A CI guard cross-references outbound third-party API hosts and *_API_KEY environment variables against the subprocessor list and fails when a vendor appears in code but not in the list.
The subprocessor page carries a last-updated date and a stated change-notification mechanism, since enterprise DPAs typically require advance notice of new subprocessors.
npm run check && npm run build pass.
userStories.notes: [LEGAL / P1] For enterprise customers an undisclosed subprocessor is usually a breach of our own DPA, separate from the GDPR Art. 13/14 and international-transfer exposure. Evidence: client/src/pages/legal/Subprocessors.tsx lists only Supabase, Google Cloud Platform, Stripe, Twilio SendGrid. Actual outbound hosts found in server/ and supabase/functions/: api.openai.com, api.anthropic.com, api.twilio.com, api.zoominfo.com, api.apollo.io, api.dataforseo.com, graph.microsoft.com, login.microsoftonline.com, quickbooks.api.intuit.com, places.googleapis.com, accounts.google.com, us1.api.mailchimp.com, plus Sentry from the frontend bundle. Credentials in use: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, CLAUDE_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN, SENDGRID_API_KEY, GOOGLE_PLACES_API_KEY, MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, APPLE_CLIENT_SECRET, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY. Good news already in place: ZoomInfo and Apollo.io ARE named in the Privacy Policy at lines 88-96; this story is about the subprocessor page and the AI gap. POLICY-COPY RULE (all LEGAL stories, decided 2026-08-17): drafting legal/policy text alongside the code IS in scope, but every changed user-facing legal string must be called out in the commit body under a FOR COUNSEL REVIEW heading so it is reviewed before deploy. IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-18. Subprocessors.tsx went from 4 providers to 19, split into two tables: 7 CORE (always in the data path: Supabase, GCP, Stripe, SendGrid, Sentry, OpenAI, Anthropic) and 12 CUSTOMER-ENABLED (Apollo, ZoomInfo, Twilio, Microsoft, Google, Apple, QuickBooks, Salesforce, Mailchimp, e-automate, PrintFleet, DataForSEO). The second table is not strictly required - those act under customer direction, not ours - but a customer working out where their data can go deserves more than the half we are obliged to publish. Added a data-categories column throughout. EVERY entry was confirmed against a real call site per the AC; four candidates were REJECTED as not data flows and recorded with reasons in the guard: HelloSign and AdobeSign (seed fixtures only - the signature send path is a stub that creates no envelope), Slack (a documentation URL in the integration catalog), Canon/HP/Xerox (seed fixture endpoints never called). MOST SIGNIFICANT DISCLOSURE: recorded service calls (routes-voice-ticket-close.ts) and meeting audio (meeting-transcription/_stt.ts) are sent to OpenAI for transcription - the audio of customer conversations leaves our systems - and imported file contents plus QBR fleet/usage/service data go to Anthropic. Neither was disclosed anywhere. Privacy Policy gains section 3.6 naming each feature and what content it sends. DELIBERATELY NOT CLAIMED: that data is not used to train third-party models. The AC allows the claim only if verified against the vendor terms in force, which cannot be done from here, so the policy points to the commercial terms and gives a contact instead of asserting it. Someone should confirm the account-level terms and then make the claim properly. GUARD: scripts/check-subprocessors.mjs (npm run check:subprocessors, wired into ci.yml) cross-references third-party hosts in server/ + supabase/functions/ AND *_API_KEY/_SECRET/_TOKEN env vars against the page, detecting 17 vendors. FIRST VERSION OF THE GUARD PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON: it substring-searched the whole page, so deleting the OpenAI table row left the name in the surrounding prose and the check stayed green. Rewritten to parse only name: entries out of the subprocessor arrays, then re-tested by deleting the OpenAI row - now correctly fails with exit 1. Worth remembering as a guard-design trap: verify a guard by breaking the thing it guards, not by watching it pass. VERIFIED: tsc holds at 1058; lint 11664 (-252); build passes; browser render of /subprocessors, /privacy and /cookies confirms the new content is actually on the page (4345/12850/3097 chars, zero JS errors).

userStories.title: Article 14 notice for contacts sourced from data enrichment
userStories.description: As a person whose contact record was bought from ZoomInfo or Apollo rather than given by me, I have a right to be told you hold my data, and today nothing in the platform generates that notice or tracks which records came from enrichment rather than from the customer.
acceptanceCriteria: Enrichment-sourced contact records are marked with their provenance (source provider and acquisition date) at write time in the enrichment paths, so indirectly-collected records are distinguishable from customer-supplied ones.
A privacy notice is reachable for those data subjects covering the GDPR Art. 14 elements: identity of the controller, categories of data, source, purposes, legal basis, retention, and their rights.
Objection and erasure requests from an enriched contact are routable through the existing GDPR request flow without requiring an account.
Suppression is durable: an erased or objecting contact is not silently re-added by the next enrichment run.

The division of controller/processor responsibility between Printyx and its tenants for enrichment data is written down in docs/ and reflected in the DPA page, since the tenant is often the controller here.
npm run check && npm run test pass.
userStories.notes: [LEGAL / P2] The harder half of the data-provider question: disclosure to CUSTOMERS is already adequate (Privacy Policy lines 88-96 name ZoomInfo and Apollo.io), disclosure to the DATA SUBJECTS whose records were purchased is entirely absent. GDPR Art. 14 gives a one-month notice window from acquisition. Enrichment call sites: server/services/lead-intelligence-service.ts, server/routes-data-enrichment.ts, server/services/integrations-service.ts, server/routes-integrations-real.ts. Note the canonical CRM object model (docs/crm-canonical-model.md): contacts are companyContacts, companies are business_records. Scope the provenance columns to the canonical tables only. This one warrants counsel input on the controller/processor split before implementation. POLICY-COPY RULE (all LEGAL stories, decided 2026-08-17): drafting legal/policy text alongside the code IS in scope, but every changed user-facing legal string must be called out in the commit body under a FOR COUNSEL REVIEW heading so it is reviewed before deploy. MOSTLY IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-18 - LEFT passes:false, see the last AC. WHAT LANDS: new shared/data-provenance-schema.ts with TWO tables and drizzle/migrations/_contact_data_provenance.sql (hand-run, same reason as LEGAL-009: journalling without a snapshot widens the COP-M00 gap). (1) contact_data_provenance records source + acquisition date + which fields the provider supplied + Art.14 notice status, keyed by subject type+id rather than an FK because the same question applies to companyContacts AND business_records and the CRM is mid-migration between duplicate models - a join table survives that, two sets of added columns would have to move with it. (2) contact_suppressions is the durable half and is DELIBERATELY NOT tied to a contact row: the row is what gets deleted, the suppression is what has to survive it, otherwise the next enrichment run re-acquires the same person from the same provider and the erasure quietly undoes itself. Keyed by lower-cased email because that is what providers match on. WIRED, not just a library: lead-intelligence-service.enrichLeadFromApollo now calls isSuppressed() BEFORE applying any provider data and returns early, and recordProvenance() after applying it. isSuppressed FAILS CLOSED - a thrown query returns true, because a missing record costs a lead and a wrongly-acquired one costs a person who formally asked to be left alone. recordProvenance upserts and NEVER walks a sent/suppressed/exempt status back to pending. Caught myself using an 'as EnrichmentResult' cast to paper over the early return missing a required field and adding two it did not declare; fixed the interface properly instead (suppressed/reason are now declared, and suppressed:false is distinguishable from enriched:false - the caller needs to tell "found nothing" from "not allowed to look"). PUBLIC NOTICE: /data-sources, reachable WITHOUT an account because the people it is for do not have one and a notice behind a login is not a notice. Covers Art.14 elements: controller identity, source (Apollo/ZoomInfo named), categories, purposes, legal basis, retention, rights, and the supervisory-authority route. Verified rendering unauthenticated (2957 chars, no JS errors). NOT MET, hence passes:false: the AC requires the controller/processor division to be WRITTEN DOWN AND REFLECTED IN THE DPA PAGE. docs/enrichment-controller-processor.md drafts the position (customer=controller, Printyx=processor) and deliberately argues against itself in a section on where that is uncomfortable - notably that Printyx may hold the provider contracts and selects the providers, which looks more like joint control for the acquisition step, and that per-tenant suppression may not match what a data subject reasonably expects from one objection. I did NOT edit DataProcessingAgreement.tsx, because changing the DPA on my own reading of a contested question is exactly the kind of legal call this workstream has been routing to a human. Counsel needs to confirm the position and four specific facts listed in the doc, then the DPA edit is a small follow-up. VERIFIED: 10 unit tests focused on suppression durability and Art.14 triggering; tsc holds at 1058; lint 11683; build passes; migration-journal and deno-schema guards green.

userStories.title: Capture consent before recording meetings
userStories.description: As a participant in a recorded meeting, I need to be asked, because supabase/functions/meeting-transcription uploads and stores audio with no consent capture anywhere in the flow, and eleven US states require all-party consent to record a conversation.
acceptanceCriteria: Recording cannot start without an affirmative, recorded consent step; the consent record persists with timestamp, actor, and scope, using the existing consent surface (server/services/consent-management-service.ts, consentRecords) rather than a new one.
Participants are given notice before capture begins, not after.
The consent state is queryable and exportable per recording, so a later dispute can be answered with evidence.
Recordings that cannot be tied to a consent record are identified; the story notes state how many exist and what is being done about them.
Retention for recordings and derived transcripts is defined and enforced by the retention engine, matching whatever the Privacy Policy states.
Erasure of a participant removes or anonymizes their recordings and transcripts (coordinate with LEGAL-004 rather than duplicating the object-deletion logic).
npm run check && npm run test pass; deno check passes on the edge functions touched.
userStories.notes: [LEGAL / P1] Not on the original question list; surfaced during the audit and carries real statutory damages. All-party-consent states include California (Penal Code 632, $5,000 statutory per violation under CIPA), Illinois, Florida, Pennsylvania, Washington, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, Connecticut, Delaware, Oregon (varies by call type). Evidence: grep -i consent across supabase/functions/meeting-transcription, server/routes-meeting*, and client/src/pages/MeetingTranscription.tsx returns zero hits. Storage bucket 'meeting-recordings' at supabase/functions/meeting-transcription/handlers/recordings.ts:15. The consent infrastructure to build on already exists at server/services/consent-management-service.ts (recordConsent, withdrawal handling, audit). POLICY-COPY RULE (all LEGAL stories, decided 2026-08-17): drafting legal/policy text alongside the code IS in scope, but every changed user-facing legal string must be called out in the commit body under a FOR COUNSEL REVIEW heading so it is reviewed before deploy. MOSTLY IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-18 - LEFT passes:false. Enforcement is done and tested; two ACs are not fully satisfiable here. WHAT LANDS: POST /meeting-transcription/upload now REFUSES to record without consentConfirmed=true, a recognized consentMethod (verbal|written|checkbox|in_meeting_announcement), and at least one named participant. Checked BEFORE any row is written and before a single byte is stored. Consent goes into the EXISTING consent_records ledger per the AC, not a new table, so withdrawal/export/erasure keep working through paths that already exist; a recording is tied to its consent via proof_reference holding the recording id, because meeting_recordings is a drift table (no Drizzle schema, no migration) and bolting a column onto it would put the evidence where nothing else looks. FAILS CLOSED throughout: if the consent insert fails the metadata row is rolled back and the upload is refused, and if the audio upload later fails the consent record is deleted too (otherwise the coverage report would claim a nonexistent recording was covered). Needs one new consent_type enum value, added in drizzle/migrations/_recording_consent.sql. THAT MIGRATION IS HAND-RUN, not journalled: I first wrote it as 0057 and journalled it, and check:migrations correctly rejected it because a journal entry with no snapshot WIDENS the known snapshot gap (25->26, COP-M00). Generating a proper snapshot needs db:generate against a live DB. So it follows the established _backfill_*.sql / _pin_storage_bucket_visibility.sql convention instead. Until it is applied uploads fail closed, which is the safe direction. ALSO: GET /recordings/:id/consent answers what consent is on file (returns consented:false with a reason rather than 404, since "nothing on file" is a meaningful answer); meeting_recordings + meeting_transcriptions added to the retention engine at 730 days; Privacy Policy gains section 3.6 on recorded meetings (AI section renumbered 3.6->3.7); erasure of the audio itself was already covered by LEGAL-004, coordinated not duplicated. NOT FULLY MET: (1) "Participants are given notice before capture begins" - enforced as far as the API can: the uploader must state the method and record the exact notice text participants heard, which is stored on the consent record. But client/src/pages/MeetingTranscription.tsx is ENTIRELY MOCK DATA (useState with hardcoded recordings, no upload wiring anywhere in client/src), so there is no capture UI to put a visible notice in. When a real recording UI is built it must show the notice before capture starts. (2) "Recordings that cannot be tied to a consent record are identified; state how many exist" - scripts/report-recording-consent-coverage.ts (npm run recordings:consent-coverage) does exactly this and deliberately deletes nothing, but it needs SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY which this environment does not have, so THE COUNT IS UNKNOWN. Someone with credentials must run it; what to do with uncovered recordings is a legal call, not a script call. VERIFIED: 14 unit tests on the consent module (refusal cases, participant parsing, notice retention, ip/user-agent capture, source mapping, failure-not-throw); 58 tests green across all six suites this workstream has added; tsc holds at 1058; lint 11669; build passes; all three touched edge files syntax-clean under esbuild; migration-journal, subprocessor and edge-path guards green.

userStories.title: Verify or remove the SOC 2 Type II compliance claim
userStories.description: As the company, we cannot assert a certification we do not hold, because 'SOC 2 Type II compliance' appears as a security measure in the Privacy Policy itself and 'SOC 2 compliance' appears on a marketing page, and nothing in the repo evidences a current Type II report.
acceptanceCriteria: Confirm whether a current SOC 2 Type II report exists, with the auditor and observation period recorded.
If it exists: keep the claim, and state the report type and period wherever it appears rather than the bare phrase.

If it does not exist: remove the claim from client/src/pages/legal/PrivacyPolicy.tsx:257 and client/src/pages/marketing/ModernArchitecture.tsx:343, and replace it with the controls actually in place, which are real and worth stating (row-level security, encryption at rest and in transit, MFA, RBAC, audit logging).
If a Type II audit is underway, any interim wording says exactly that ('SOC 2 Type II audit in progress, report expected <date>') and never implies a completed certification.
Every other certification or framework claim in client/src is checked the same way (ISO 27001, PCI DSS, HIPAA, 'GDPR compliant'), and each is substantiated or removed.
A CI grep guard fails the build when an unapproved certification claim string is reintroduced.
npm run check && npm run build pass.
userStories.notes: [LEGAL / P1] A false certification claim is a clean FTC Section 5 deceptive-practice case and this one sits inside a legal document, which is the worst place for it. Evidence: client/src/pages/legal/PrivacyPolicy.tsx:257 ('SOC 2 Type II compliance and industry-standard security frameworks', listed among security measures in section 5.1) and client/src/pages/marketing/ModernArchitecture.tsx:343 ('Row-level security, encrypted data at rest and in transit, SOC 2 compliance...'). NEEDS A HUMAN ANSWER: does the report exist? Do not guess. If unanswered when this story is picked up, remove the claim, since removing a true claim is recoverable and keeping a false one is not. DECIDED 2026-08-17 by Dj Pearson: NO SOC 2 Type II report exists. Remove the claim from PrivacyPolicy.tsx:257 and ModernArchitecture.tsx:343 and replace with the controls actually in place and verifiable in the codebase: row-level security, encryption at rest and in transit, MFA, RBAC, audit logging. Do not substitute another certification claim. This resolves the human-decision blocker on this story. POLICY-COPY RULE (all LEGAL stories, decided 2026-08-17): drafting legal/policy text alongside the code IS in scope, but every changed user-facing legal string must be called out in the commit body under a FOR COUNSEL REVIEW heading so it is reviewed before deploy. IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-18 per the recorded decision (no report exists, remove the claim). The story named TWO sites; there were FIVE, and the three it missed were the worse ones. Removed from: PrivacyPolicy.tsx (inside a legal document), ModernArchitecture.tsx (marketing), AND Login.tsx (the PUBLIC login screen, unauthenticated), plus two fabricated compliance DASHBOARDS - admin/SystemSecurity.tsx hardcoded green Compliant badges for SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, GDPR and CCPA next to invented audit scores (98/100, 95/100, 99/100, 87/100), and BusinessProcessOptimization.tsx hardcoded ISO 9001:2015 and SOC 2 Type II as Compliant with invented scores (96.7%, 94.2%), audit dates (Nov 2024, Sep 2024) and non-conformity counts (2, 1). None of it came from data - no useQuery, no API, pure literals. The dashboards are the more dangerous half: staff answer customer security questionnaires from what the product tells them, so a fabricated compliance screen becomes a written misrepresentation with a straight face. Both panels now state plainly that no report is held, that nothing tracks certification status, and list the controls that ARE real and verifiable in the platform (row-level security tenant isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, MFA, RBAC, audit logging) so a questionnaire can be answered from something true. Checked the whole client for the other frameworks per the AC: ISO 27001, ISO 9001, PCI DSS, FedRAMP, HIPAA-compliant, GDPR-compliant, CCPA-compliant - all now clean. GUARD: scripts/check-certification-claims.mjs (npm run check:certifications, wired into ci.yml) fails on any unapproved certification claim in client/src, with an APPROVED list that is deliberately EMPTY so obtaining a certification means adding it there with its report period and auditor in the same commit that publishes the claim. Disclaimer markers keep it from flagging its own fix. Proven to fire by restoring the exact Login.tsx wording: exits 1 naming the file and line. VERIFIED: tsc holds at 1058; lint 11669; build passes; all five guards green; browser render of /login, /privacy and /modern-architecture confirms no SOC 2 / ISO 27001 string survives in the rendered output (964/13573/5236 chars, zero JS errors).

userStories.title: Send a cancellation confirmation and keep a durable cancellation record
userStories.description: As a subscriber who just cancelled, I need written confirmation, because several state auto-renewal statutes require an acknowledgement of cancellation and no cancellation email is sent today, even though the cancellation flow itself is well built.
acceptanceCriteria: Cancelling sends an immediate confirmation email stating what was cancelled, whether it takes effect immediately or at period end, the exact effective date, and what happens to the customer's data afterward.
The confirmation is also visible in-app, so it does not depend on email delivery succeeding.
A durable cancellation record is written (who, when, immediate vs period-end, effective date), retrievable later as evidence that cancellation was honored.

The data-handling sentence in the email matches the actual post-termination behavior implemented in LEGAL-005; if that story has not landed, the email states current behavior truthfully rather than the aspirational policy.
A test asserts both cancellation modes produce a record and enqueue a confirmation.
npm run check && npm run test pass.
userStories.notes: [LEGAL / P3] The cancellation flow itself PASSED the audit and needs no redesign: client/src/pages/SubscriptionSettings.tsx:205-235 offers cancel-immediately and cancel-at-period-end in one dialog, reachable self-serve, same medium as signup, with no retention gauntlet. That satisfies the click-to-cancel structure. The only gap is the acknowledgement: grep for cancel + email/notification in server/services/subscription-service.ts returns nothing. Cancel API at server/routes-subscriptions.ts:242. Notification helper to reuse: SubscriptionService.createNotification with channels ['in_app','email'], as used by the trial reminders at subscription-service.ts:780. POLICY-COPY RULE (all LEGAL stories, decided 2026-08-17): drafting legal/policy text alongside the code IS in scope, but every changed user-facing legal string must be called out in the commit body under a FOR COUNSEL REVIEW heading so it is reviewed before deploy. IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-18. CORRECTION TO MY OWN AUDIT: this story's note said 'no durable cancellation record' and 'no cancellation email'. Both were partly wrong and the real defect was narrower and more interesting. cancelSubscription ALREADY wrote a subscription_events row (durable record, real) AND a subscription_notifications row with channels ['in_app','email']. The in-app half worked. The email half did not: nothing anywhere reads subscription_notifications with status='pending' and sends it - the table is only INSERTed and then READ by the in-app list endpoint in routes-subscriptions.ts. So the channels array was a recorded intention with no mechanism behind it, exactly the same shape as the cookie banner in LEGAL-001. WHAT LANDS: new server/services/cancellation-confirmation.ts builds and sends a real confirmation through the existing email-service (the working path, same one the trial emails use), stating what was cancelled, whether it was immediate or end-of-period, the exact effective date, and that no further charge will be made. The event record now carries mode, effectiveDate, canceledAt, planId, AND whether the confirmation actually reached anyone (confirmationSent/confirmationRecipient/confirmationError) - a cancellation record has to answer, months later and to someone hostile, what happened and whether the customer was told. The in-app notification message gained the effective date and the no-further-charge sentence so it does not depend on email delivery. Sending never throws: a cancellation that succeeded must not report failure because the mail server was down, but the failure is logged and recorded on the event rather than swallowed. DELIBERATE WORDING CHOICE: dataHandlingSentence describes CURRENT behavior (export window open for 30 days, then deletion except stated categories) rather than the aspirational policy, because LEGAL-005's purge ships report-only until someone sets TENANT_PURGE_ENABLED=true. Promising completed deletion in an email would be the same class of untrue statement this workstream exists to remove, and there is a test asserting the sentence does not claim deletion has already happened. VERIFIED: 9 unit tests on the email content (effective date present in subject/text/html, immediate vs end-of-period distinguished, no-further-charge stated, org named, misuse contact given, plan name optional without leaving double spaces, export deadline arithmetic, retained categories named); tsc holds at 1058; lint 11683; build passes; full server suite 2005 passed with only the 2 known pre-existing universal-search failures.

userStories.title: Crisis-response guardrail before any AI surface is exposed outside authentication
userStories.description: As the company, we need a defined safety response before an AI conversational surface can reach anyone outside our authenticated B2B users, because no crisis handling exists anywhere in the codebase and the chatbot is one route change away from being public.
acceptanceCriteria: A documented policy states which AI surfaces may be exposed unauthenticated and what safety handling each requires before that can happen.

System prompts for any conversational surface include instructions to respond to self-harm, crisis, or emergency disclosures with appropriate resources and to not continue the sales or support script in that turn.
The response surfaces region-appropriate crisis resources (988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US) rather than a generic deflection.
A CI or review guard flags removal of requireAuth from any chatbot or conversational AI route, so public exposure is a deliberate decision rather than a diff nobody noticed.
Tests cover a handful of crisis-phrasing inputs and assert the guardrail response, so a prompt edit cannot silently drop it.
npm run check && npm run test pass.
userStories.notes: [LEGAL / P3, deliberately low] Correctly scoped as low priority TODAY: the chatbot is authenticated internal B2B (every route in server/routes-chatbot.ts uses requireAuth + resolveTenant, e.g. line 831), there is no public widget, and the only unauthenticated surface is the marketing ROI calculator (supabase/functions/public-calculator), which is not conversational. grep for self-harm|suicide|crisis|988|hotline across server, supabase/functions, and client/src returns zero. This becomes urgent the day the chatbot is exposed to end customers or a public widget ships; the CI guard is the part worth having now, because it converts a silent risk into a visible decision. POLICY-COPY RULE (all LEGAL stories, decided 2026-08-17): drafting legal/policy text alongside the code IS in scope, but every changed user-facing legal string must be called out in the commit body under a FOR COUNSEL REVIEW heading so it is reviewed before deploy. IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-18. Confirmed the original low-priority assessment before building: /api/chatbot/query still has requireAuth, and an audit of ALL nine unauthenticated edge functions (client-metrics, csrf-token, hello, mobile-auth, oauth-proxy, public-booking, public-calculator, public-forms, signup) found none of them conversational. So there is no public surface today; the guardrail exists so it predates the exposure rather than being remembered after it. TWO LAYERS, deliberately. (1) DETERMINISTIC detector in server/lib/crisis-response.ts, called in routes-chatbot BEFORE any retrieval or model call. A system-prompt instruction is a request to a model that a prompt edit, model swap or long conversation can erode; the detector does not care. (2) CRISIS_SYSTEM_DIRECTIVE appended via withCrisisGuardrail() to the three conversational prompts (gpt5-service support, ai-employee-service support, deal-desk copilot), for what the detector misses. Data-processing prompts (CSV mapping, email parsing, OCR, dedup) were deliberately EXCLUDED - nobody is talking to them, and a directive there is noise that trains people to ignore it where it matters. The directive instructs the model to STOP the task and NOT to refuse, because a refusal is its own unsafe response: someone disclosing distress who gets 'I cannot discuss that' has been shut out at the worst moment. Resources are specific (988, 741741, 911), not a gesture at getting help. GUARD: scripts/check-ai-safety.mjs (npm run check:ai-safety, wired into ci.yml) enforces both that the chatbot route keeps requireAuth and that conversational prompts keep the guardrail. FIRST VERSION OF RULE 2 PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON - it searched for the bare identifier 'withCrisisGuardrail', which survives in the import line after the call site is removed, so the simulated regression stayed green. Tightened to match the CALL. That is the SECOND time this session a guard passed on a surviving substring (LEGAL-007 was the first): verify a guard by breaking the thing it guards, every time. TESTS: 33, and the 10 false-positive cases matter as much as the 13 true positives - a detector that fires on 'this deadline is killing me' or 'the printer is dead again' trains people to ignore it, and an ignored safety response is worse than none because it looks like coverage. docs/ai-surface-exposure-policy.md lists six prerequisites before any public exposure, including that CRISIS_RESOURCES_US is US-only and showing a US number to someone abroad is worse than showing nothing. VERIFIED: tsc holds at 1058; lint 11683; build passes; all six guards green; full server suite 2038 passed with only the 2 known pre-existing universal-search failures.
